newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam says upgrading bean quality poses problems.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam says upgrading bean quality poses problems.

text.p: Vietnam is finding it difficult to impose quality standards to upgrade the quality of its coffee beans, an official said on Tuesday.

Hoang Anh, director of Cafecontrol Vietnam, told the Third Asia International Coffee conference here industry-wide standards have been adopted in the country to ensure "rejection of all kinds of defects in the product."

"The state coffee farms now are applying progressive techniques in cultivation and product processing, but this is still not widespread since nearly 80 percent of the national coffee output comes from private farmers," Hoang said.
He said more technicians should be trained to manage the quality of coffee produced by Vietnam.
Vietnam, the second biggest producer of robusta coffee in Asia after Indonesia, has often run into problems regarding the quality of its beans.
Heavy rains which pounded the southern Dak Lak growing region this season kindled concerns in the trade about mould hitting the crop.
Dak Lak produced about two-thirds of the estimated 240,000-270,000 tonnes Vietnam exported during its 1996-97 (November/January) harvest season.
Vietnam has denied that mould affected its crop while urging exporters to pay more attention to quality.
Hoang estimated that 15-20 percent of the crop is adversely affected by rains coming in the later part of the year.
"Continuously rainy days often affect the product quality at the beginning of the crop," the official said.
Regional coffee traders said the beans shipped out in November will begin to reach roasters in the U.S. and Europe this month.
Any concerns about the quality of Vietnamese beans will become apparent by then, they said.
